claim: Sepsis accounts for one in every two to three deaths that occur in hospitals in the United States.
source: Sepsis is a common cause of morbidity and mortality in the United States, accounting for one in every two to three deaths that occur in hospitals (Martin et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Martin et al., 2003

claim: The risk of sepsis is approximately 60% higher for Black patients compared to White patients.
source: The risk of sepsis and associated mortality are approximately 60% and 80% higher, respectively, for Black patients compared to White patients (Martin et al., 2003; Prest et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Martin et al., 2003 and Prest et al., 2021

claim: Sepsis-associated mortality is approximately 80% higher for Black patients compared to White patients.
source: The risk of sepsis and associated mortality are approximately 60% and 80% higher, respectively, for Black patients compared to White patients (Martin et al., 2003; Prest et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Martin et al., 2003 and Prest et al., 2021

claim: The higher incidence of sepsis in Black individuals persists after adjustment for comorbidities and socioeconomic status.
source: The higher incidence of sepsis in Black individuals persists after adjustment for comorbidities and socioeconomic status, encompassing both a greater risk for developing infection, and once infected, a greater risk of organ dysfunction (Mayr et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mayr et al., 2010

claim: Variants in the apolipoprotein L1 gene (APOL1), common in people of African ancestry, are associated with sepsis incidence and severity.
source: Recent work in the Million Veteran Program (MVP) found that variants in the apolipoprotein L1 gene (APOL1), common in people of African ancestry, are associated with sepsis incidence and severity (Wu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wu et al., 2021

claim: Two genetic variants in APOL1—termed G1 (rs73885319/rs60910145) and G2 (rs71785313)—are found almost exclusively in individuals of African ancestry.
source: Two genetic variants in APOL1—termed G1 (rs73885319/rs60910145) and G2 (rs71785313)—are found almost exclusively in individuals of African ancestry and confer resistance to Trypanosoma brucei infection (Genovese et al., 2010; O'Toole et al., 2017; Tzur et al., 2010; Lipkowitz et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Genovese et al., 2010; O'Toole et al., 2017; Tzur et al., 2010; Lipkowitz et al., 2013

claim: APOL1 G1 and G2 variants confer resistance to Trypanosoma brucei infection.
source: Two genetic variants in APOL1—termed G1 (rs73885319/rs60910145) and G2 (rs71785313)—are found almost exclusively in individuals of African ancestry and confer resistance to Trypanosoma brucei infection (Genovese et al., 2010; O'Toole et al., 2017; Tzur et al., 2010; Lipkowitz et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Genovese et al., 2010; O'Toole et al., 2017; Tzur et al., 2010; Lipkowitz et al., 2013

claim: Individuals carrying two APOL1 risk alleles have a marked increase in the risk of chronic renal disease.
source: However, individuals carrying two such alleles (i.e., G1/G1, G1/G2, or G2/G2) have a marked increase in the risk of chronic renal disease; for example, among African-Americans, individuals carrying two APOL1 risk alleles are 7.3 times more likely to develop hypertension-associated end-stage renal disease (ESRD) compared to those without two risk alleles (Genovese et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Genovese et al., 2010

claim: Among African-Americans, individuals carrying two APOL1 risk alleles are 7.3 times more likely to develop hypertension-associated end-stage renal disease (ESRD) compared to those without two risk alleles.
source: However, individuals carrying two such alleles (i.e., G1/G1, G1/G2, or G2/G2) have a marked increase in the risk of chronic renal disease; for example, among African-Americans, individuals carrying two APOL1 risk alleles are 7.3 times more likely to develop hypertension-associated end-stage renal disease (ESRD) compared to those without two risk alleles (Genovese et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Genovese et al., 2010

claim: Carriage of two APOL1 risk alleles is associated with an increased prevalence of hypertension, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, and HIV-associated nephropathy.
source: Correspondingly, carriage of two risk alleles is associated with an increased prevalence of numerous renal-related disorders, including hypertension, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, and HIV-associated nephropathy (Foster et al., 2013; Freedman et al., 2018; Kopp et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Foster et al., 2013; Freedman et al., 2018; Kopp et al., 2011

claim: APOL1 high-risk alleles typically follow a pattern of recessive expression.
source: While these high-risk alleles typically follow a pattern of recessive expression (i.e., without increased risk for individuals carrying a single allele), because their carriage rates are so high among African-Americans (10–15% of African-Americans carry two APOL1 risk alleles), a substantial portion of this population faces increased APOL1-related risk (Genovese et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Genovese et al., 2010

claim: 10–15% of African-Americans carry two APOL1 risk alleles.
source: While these high-risk alleles typically follow a pattern of recessive expression (i.e., without increased risk for individuals carrying a single allele), because their carriage rates are so high among African-Americans (10–15% of African-Americans carry two APOL1 risk alleles), a substantial portion of this population faces increased APOL1-related risk (Genovese et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Genovese et al., 2010

claim: The APOL1 risk variants are considered gain-of-injury variants.
source: The specific mechanisms whereby the APOL1 risk variants increase the risk for renal disease are not fully understood, but beyond their role in innate immunity and resistance to trypanosomiasis, the APOL1 risk variants are considered gain-of-injury variants (Kruzel-Davila et al., 2016), intensifying autophagy, cell death, endothelial cell inflammation and dysfunction, and immune pathway activation (Wu et al., 2021; Friedman and Pollak, 2020; Daneshpajouhnejad et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kruzel-Davila et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2021; Friedman and Pollak, 2020; Daneshpajouhnejad et al., 2022

claim: APOL1 risk variants intensify autophagy, cell death, endothelial cell inflammation and dysfunction, and immune pathway activation.
source: The specific mechanisms whereby the APOL1 risk variants increase the risk for renal disease are not fully understood, but beyond their role in innate immunity and resistance to trypanosomiasis, the APOL1 risk variants are considered gain-of-injury variants (Kruzel-Davila et al., 2016), intensifying autophagy, cell death, endothelial cell inflammation and dysfunction, and immune pathway activation (Wu et al., 2021; Friedman and Pollak, 2020; Daneshpajouhnejad et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wu et al., 2021; Friedman and Pollak, 2020; Daneshpajouhnejad et al., 2022

claim: Many patients with two APOL1 risk variants never develop renal disease.
source: However, many patients with two APOL1 risk variants never develop renal disease, leading researchers to propose a two-hit model in which genetic susceptibility combined with an inflammatory trigger leads to disease (Kruzel-Davila et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kruzel-Davila et al., 2016

claim: A two-hit model has been proposed in which genetic susceptibility combined with an inflammatory trigger leads to APOL1-related disease.
source: However, many patients with two APOL1 risk variants never develop renal disease, leading researchers to propose a two-hit model in which genetic susceptibility combined with an inflammatory trigger leads to disease (Kruzel-Davila et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kruzel-Davila et al., 2016

claim: APOL1 expression is induced by inflammatory cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor alpha and gamma-interferon.
source: Indeed, APOL1 expression is induced by inflammatory cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor alpha and gamma-interferon (Limou et al., 2015; Nichols et al., 2015); thus increased transcription of the gain-of-function variant APOL1 is most likely to occur in the setting of severe infection.
evidence: Supported by citations to Limou et al., 2015; Nichols et al., 2015

claim: Increased transcription of the gain-of-function variant APOL1 is most likely to occur in the setting of severe infection.
source: Indeed, APOL1 expression is induced by inflammatory cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor alpha and gamma-interferon (Limou et al., 2015; Nichols et al., 2015); thus increased transcription of the gain-of-function variant APOL1 is most likely to occur in the setting of severe infection.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the induction of APOL1 by inflammatory cytokines

claim: APOL1 is associated with renal disease.
source: More specifically, since APOL1 is associated with renal disease (Foster et al., 2013; Bajaj et al., 2020; Yusuf et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021) and existing renal disease is associated with worse sepsis outcomes (Doi et al., 2008) (including increased kidney injury), the relationship between APOL1 and sepsis external to existing renal disease remains unclear.
evidence: Supported by citations to Foster et al., 2013; Bajaj et al., 2020; Yusuf et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021

claim: Existing renal disease is associated with worse sepsis outcomes.
source: More specifically, since APOL1 is associated with renal disease (Foster et al., 2013; Bajaj et al., 2020; Yusuf et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021) and existing renal disease is associated with worse sepsis outcomes (Doi et al., 2008) (including increased kidney injury), the relationship between APOL1 and sepsis external to existing renal disease remains unclear.
evidence: Supported by citation to Doi et al., 2008

claim: Several inhibitors of APOL1 are in various stages of development.
source: In particular, several inhibitors of APOL1 are in various stages of development—if APOL1 high-risk genotypes are directly associated with the pathogenesis of sepsis external to pre-existing severe renal disease or other organ system dysfunction, such drugs could be offered to high-risk patients to prevent or treat the occurrence of sepsis in scenarios of acute infection (Friedman et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Friedman et al., 2022

claim: The study cohort included 2242 Black patients hospitalized with an infection.
source: The primary cohort included 2242 Black patients hospitalized with an infection; 361 (16.1%) patients carried a high-risk APOL1 genotype and 1881 (83.9%) carried low-risk genotypes (Table 1).
evidence: Direct statement of study cohort size

claim: 361 (16.1%) patients in the cohort carried a high-risk APOL1 genotype.
source: The primary cohort included 2242 Black patients hospitalized with an infection; 361 (16.1%) patients carried a high-risk APOL1 genotype and 1881 (83.9%) carried low-risk genotypes (Table 1).
evidence: Direct statement of genotype distribution in the cohort

claim: 1881 (83.9%) patients in the cohort carried low-risk APOL1 genotypes.
source: The primary cohort included 2242 Black patients hospitalized with an infection; 361 (16.1%) patients carried a high-risk APOL1 genotype and 1881 (83.9%) carried low-risk genotypes (Table 1).

claim: The baseline characteristics of patients with high- and low-risk APOL1 genotypes did not differ significantly in age, sex, and most general medical comorbidities and infection types.
source: The baseline characteristics of patients with the high- and low-risk genotypes did not differ significantly in age, sex, and most general medical comorbidities and infection types.
evidence: Based on statistical comparison of baseline characteristics

claim: Renal-related comorbidities were significantly more frequent in the high-risk APOL1 genotype group (p=1.60 × 10–10).
source: However, renal-related comorbidities were significantly more frequent in the high-risk genotype group (p=1.60 × 10–10) (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis with p-value

claim: Of 2242 Black patients hospitalized with infections, 565 developed sepsis.
source: Within the primary cohort of patients hospitalized with infections, 565 patients developed sepsis, including 105 (29.1%) with APOL1 high-risk genotypes and 460 (24.5%) with low-risk genotypes.
evidence: Direct statement of outcome data

claim: 105 (29.1%) patients with APOL1 high-risk genotypes developed sepsis.
source: Within the primary cohort of patients hospitalized with infections, 565 patients developed sepsis, including 105 (29.1%) with APOL1 high-risk genotypes and 460 (24.5%) with low-risk genotypes.

claim: 460 (24.5%) patients with low-risk APOL1 genotypes developed sepsis.

claim: The risk of sepsis was significantly increased among patients with the high-risk APOL1 genotypes (OR = 1.29 [95% CI, 1.00–1.67; p=0.047]).
source: The risk of sepsis was significantly increased among patients with the high-risk APOL1 genotypes (OR = 1.29 [95% CI, 1.00–1.67; p=0.047]) (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by logistic regression analysis with statistical significance

claim: The association between sepsis and APOL1 high-risk genotypes was not significant after adjustment for pre-existing severe renal disease (OR = 1.14 [95% CI: 0.88–1.48; p=0.33]).
source: However, the association between sepsis and APOL1 high-risk genotypes was not significant after adjustment for pre-existing severe renal disease (OR = 1.14 [95% CI: 0.88–1.48; p=0.33]), nor after exclusion of those patients (n=458) with severe renal disease (OR = 0.99 [95% CI, 0.70–1.39; p=0.95]) (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by adjusted logistic regression analysis

claim: The association between sepsis and APOL1 high-risk genotypes was not significant after exclusion of patients with severe renal disease (OR = 0.99 [95% CI, 0.70–1.39; p=0.95]).

evidence: Supported by logistic regression analysis in subset of patients

claim: There was no association between sepsis and APOL1 high-risk genotypes in analysis of patients with severe renal disease alone (OR = 1.29 [95% CI, 0.84–1.98, p=0.25]).
source: We also found no association between sepsis and APOL1 high-risk genotypes in analysis of patients with severe renal disease alone (OR = 1.29 [95% CI, 0.84–1.98, p=0.25]).

claim: In the restricted PheWAS performed in Black participants in BioVU (n=14,713), APOL1 high-risk genotypes were associated with infection of internal prosthetic device (OR = 1.68 [95% CI, 1.32–2.13; p=2.23 × 10–5]).

evidence: Supported by PheWAS analysis with statistical significance

claim: The associations between APOL1 and sepsis-related phenotypes were nullified after excluding individuals with pre-existing severe renal disease (n=12,547).
source: However, in an expansion of the original approach, the associations between APOL1 and sepsis-related phenotypes were nullified after we excluded individuals with pre-existing severe renal disease (n=2166) and reran the analyses (n=12,547, Figure 3, panel B).
evidence: Supported by PheWAS analysis in subset of patients without severe renal disease

claim: The findings of an overall increased sepsis risk are consistent with a recent cohort study performed in the MVP which found that high-risk APOL1 genotypes were associated with ~40% increased risk of sepsis compared to low-risk genotype patients.
source: Our findings of an overall increased sepsis risk are consistent with a recent cohort study performed in the MVP which found that high-risk APOL1 genotypes were associated with ~40% increased risk of sepsis compared to low-risk genotype patients, remaining significant after adjustment for age, sex, and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) (Wu et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citation to Wu et al., 2021

claim: In the MVP study, APOL1 is highly expressed in the endothelium.
source: Additional mechanistic analysis in this study observed that APOL1 is highly expressed in the endothelium and that the high-risk variants were associated with increased inflammation, endothelial leakage, and sepsis severity (Wu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wu et al., 2021

claim: In the MVP study, APOL1 high-risk variants were associated with increased inflammation, endothelial leakage, and sepsis severity.
source: Additional mechanistic analysis in this study observed that APOL1 is highly expressed in the endothelium and that the high-risk variants were associated with increased inflammation, endothelial leakage, and sepsis severity (Wu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wu et al., 2021

claim: Pre-existing severe renal disease is a potent risk factor for infection, sepsis, and infection-related mortality.
source: However, the association between APOL1 high-risk genotypes and sepsis is driven largely by the presence of pre-existing severe renal disease—a potent risk factor for infection, sepsis, and infection-related mortality (Sarnak and Jaber, 2000; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sarnak and Jaber, 2000; Wang et al., 2011

claim: In another MVP study that excluded patients with severe pre-existing renal dysfunction and examined the effects of APOL1 genotypes on outcomes among patients hospitalized with COVID-19 infections, high-risk APOL1 genotypes were more strongly associated with acute kidney injury than the need for mechanical ventilation or vasopressors.
source: These findings more closely parallel those of another MVP study that excluded patients with severe pre-existing renal dysfunction and examined the effects of APOL1 genotypes on outcomes among patients hospitalized with COVID-19 infections. In that study, high-risk APOL1 genotypes were more strongly associated with acute kidney injury (Hung et al., 2022) than the need for mechanical ventilation or vasopressors.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hung et al., 2022

claim: The vast majority of community acquired sepsis cases (87%) are present on admission to hospital.
source: Because the vast majority of community acquired sepsis cases (87%) are present on admission to hospital (Rhee et al., 2017), we studied sepsis occurring within 1 day of hospital admission (days –1, 0, and +1) to minimize the confounding effects of sepsis occurring secondary to procedures or events in the hospital.
evidence: Supported by citation to Rhee et al., 2017

claim: The EHR-based Sepsis-3 algorithm has a specificity of 98.1% and a sensitivity of 69.7%.
source: The algorithm uses billing codes and clinical criteria, with a specificity of 98.1% and a sensitivity of 69.7% (Rhee et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rhee et al., 2017

claim: ICD codes for septic shock or severe sepsis (ICD-9-CM, 995.92 and 785.52; ICD-10-CM, R65.20 and R65.21) are highly specific (99.3%).
source: In brief, individuals in the infection cohort met the definition of sepsis if they had either ICD codes for septic shock or severe sepsis (ICD-9-CM, 995.92 and 785.52; ICD-10-CM, R65.20 and R65.21) because these are highly specific (99.3%) (Rhee et al., 2017), or they met any Sepsis-3 criterion for serious organ dysfunction (Liu et al., 2023; Rhee et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rhee et al., 2017

claim: APOL1 high-risk genotypes were associated with an increased risk of sepsis in patients hospitalized with infections.
source: This retrospective cohort study found that APOL1 high-risk genotypes were significantly associated with an increased risk of sepsis in patients hospitalized with infections; however, this association was explained predominantly by the presence of pre-existing severe renal disease.
evidence: Supported by the study's primary analysis showing OR = 1.29 [95% CI, 1.00–1.67; p=0.047]

claim: The association between APOL1 high-risk genotypes and sepsis was explained predominantly by the presence of pre-existing severe renal disease.
source: This retrospective cohort study found that APOL1 high-risk genotypes were significantly associated with an increased risk of sepsis in patients hospitalized with infections; however, this association was explained predominantly by the presence of pre-existing severe renal disease.
evidence: Supported by analyses showing attenuation and nullification of association after adjustment for or exclusion of patients with severe renal disease

claim: Renal dysfunction was the only sepsis-associated organ dysfunction significantly associated with APOL1 high-risk genotypes.
source: Renal dysfunction was the only sepsis-associated organ dysfunction significantly associated with APOL1 high-risk genotypes, and this risk was attenuated by adjustment for pre-existing severe renal comorbidity and nullified by the exclusion of patients with pre-existing severe renal disease.
evidence: Supported by analyses showing significant association with renal dysfunction (OR = 1.64) but not other organ dysfunctions

claim: The risk of renal dysfunction associated with APOL1 high-risk genotypes was attenuated by adjustment for pre-existing severe renal comorbidity and nullified by the exclusion of patients with pre-existing severe renal disease.
source: Renal dysfunction was the only sepsis-associated organ dysfunction significantly associated with APOL1 high-risk genotypes, and this risk was attenuated by adjustment for pre-existing severe renal comorbidity and nullified by the exclusion of patients with pre-existing severe renal disease.
evidence: Supported by analyses showing OR = 1.36 after adjustment and OR = 1.16 after exclusion

claim: There appeared to be no increased risk of sepsis for carriage of high-risk genotypes among patients with pre-existing severe renal disease.
source: Moreover, there appeared to be no increased risk of sepsis for carriage of high-risk genotypes among patients with pre-existing severe renal disease.
evidence: Supported by analysis in patients with severe renal disease alone showing OR = 1.29 [95% CI, 0.84–1.98, p=0.25]

claim: The lack of association independent of pre-existing severe renal disease suggests that APOL1 high-risk genotypes are not acutely causal of sepsis beyond their association with renal disease and impaired renal function.
source: The lack of association independent of pre-existing severe renal disease suggests that APOL1 high-risk genotypes are not acutely causal of sepsis beyond their association with renal disease and impaired renal function (which, in turn, increases susceptibility to sepsis).
evidence: Based on inference from the study's findings showing no association after accounting for renal disease

claim: Drug therapies in development to prevent and treat diseases associated with APOL1 high-risk genotypes might primarily affect the renal vulnerabilities that increase risk of sepsis, rather than immediate prevention of sepsis or acute treatment of sepsis once hospitalized.
source: These results suggest that drug therapies in development to prevent and treat diseases associated with APOL1 high-risk genotypes might primarily affect the renal vulnerabilities that increase risk of sepsis, rather than immediate prevention of sepsis or acute treatment of sepsis once hospitalized.
evidence: Based on inference from the study's findings and implications for treatment

claim: APOL1 high-risk genotypes were associated with an increased risk of sepsis; however, this increased risk was attributable predominantly to pre-existing severe renal disease.
source: Conclusions:APOL1 high-risk genotypes were associated with an increased risk of sepsis; however, this increased risk was attributable predominantly to pre-existing severe renal disease.
evidence: Conclusion statement based on the study's findings
